The first fraction is \(\frac{3[-8 - (-4)]}{-2} = \frac{-12}{-2} = 6\). Using \(7^0 = 1\), the second fraction is \(\frac{-27 + 3}{8 - 2(1)} = \frac{-24}{6} = -4\), giving \(6 - (-4) = 10\).

Inside the square bracket, \(2^3 - 3^2 = 8 - 9 = -1\), giving the first fraction as \(\frac{-3(-1) + 7}{2} = 5\). The second fraction simplifies to \(\frac{16 - 4}{1 - 4} = \frac{12}{-3} = -4\), so \(5 - (-4) = 9\).
The first fraction simplifies to \(\frac{-2(-3)^2 + 10}{-4} = \frac{-18 + 10}{-4} = 2\). In the second fraction, \(-3^2 = -9\), so \(\frac{-9 + 1}{2} = -4\), giving \(2 - (-4) = 6\).
In the numerator, calculate the power and multiply to get \(-3(8) + 4 = -24 + 4 = -20\). In the denominator, multiply to get \(15 - 20 = -5\), then divide: \(-20 \div (-5) = 4\).
Evaluate the exponent and multiply in the numerator to get \(2(16) - 5 = 27\). In the denominator, multiply before adding to get \(18 - 9 = 9\), then divide: \(27 \div 9 = 3\).
In the numerator, evaluate the exponent and multiply to get \(5(9) - 5 = 40\). In the denominator, multiply to get \(22 - 18 = 4\), then divide: \(40 \div 4 = 10\).
Evaluate the exponent and multiply in the numerator to get \(-2(25) + 8 = -50 + 8 = -42\). In the denominator, multiply first to get \(14 - 21 = -7\), then divide: \(-42 \div (-7) = 6\).
In the numerator, evaluate the exponent and multiply to get \(5(8) + (-8) = 40 - 8 = 32\). In the denominator, multiply before adding to get \(12 + (-8) = 4\), then divide: \(32 \div 4 = 8\).
In the numerator, work from the inside out to get \(-4[5 - 2(9)] = -4[-13] = 52\). In the denominator, \(-2^4 = -16\) and \(3(1)^2 = 3\), giving \(-16 + 3 = -13\), so \(52 \div (-13) = -4\).

In the numerator, simplify inside the brackets to get \([9 - 8]^3 - (-5) = 1^3 + 5 = 6\). In the denominator, evaluate the bracket to get \(-2(7 - 16) - 15 = -2(-9) - 15 = 18 - 15 = 3\), then divide: \(6 \div 3 = 2\).

Simplify inside the square brackets in the numerator: \(2[3(-2)^2 - 4] - 6 = 2[12 - 4] - 6 = 10\). In the denominator, evaluate the power and brackets to get \(-8 - 3(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2\), then divide: \(10 \div (-2) = -5\).
In the numerator, \(-3^2 = -9\) and the bracket simplifies to \(2[-4 - (-1)] = 2[-3] = -6\), giving \(-9 + (-6) = -15\). In the denominator, \((-3)^2 - 4 = 9 - 4 = 5\), giving \(-15 \div 5 = -3\).

In the numerator, evaluate the powers and brackets to get \(-2(4) + 3(-8) = -8 - 24 = -32\). In the denominator, simplify inside the parentheses first to get \(2(14 - 12) - 6 = 4 - 6 = -2\), then divide: \(-32 \div (-2) = 16\).
Simplify the powers and numerators to get \(\frac{24}{-3} - \frac{-12}{-2}\). Dividing each fraction yields \(-8 - 6 = -14\).
Calculate powers and numerators to get \(\frac{100}{-25} - \frac{-6}{3}\). Dividing yields \(-4 - (-2) = -4 + 2 = -2\).
Evaluating the powers gives \(\frac{64 - 4}{-5} - \frac{7 - 16}{3} = \frac{60}{-5} - \frac{-9}{3}\). Dividing gives \(-12 - (-3) = -12 + 3 = -9\).
First evaluate the exponents and numerators: \(\frac{32 - 8}{-4} - \frac{14 - 16}{2} = \frac{24}{-4} - \frac{-2}{2}\). Performing the divisions yields \(-6 - (-1) = -6 + 1 = -5\).
Evaluate exponents to get \(\frac{27 - 7}{-4} - \frac{22 - 64}{7} = \frac{20}{-4} - \frac{-42}{7}\). Dividing gives \(-5 - (-6) = -5 + 6 = 1\).

The first fraction simplifies to \(\frac{-27 - 5(-3)}{2 - 8} = \frac{-12}{-6} = 2\). The second fraction simplifies to \(\frac{[-2(9) + 10]^2}{-4} = \frac{(-8)^2}{-4} = \frac{64}{-4} = -16\). Subtracting gives \(2 - (-16) = 18\).

Inside the square brackets, \(\frac{15}{-5} - (1 - 8) = -3 - (-7) = 4\), so the first term is \(-2(4) = -8\). The second fraction simplifies to \(\frac{3(9) - 3}{3 - 9} = \frac{24}{-6} = -4\), giving \(-8 - (-4) = -4\).
Evaluating each term separately gives \(\frac{-32 - 8}{-5} = 8\), \(\frac{4(-7) + 8}{-5} = 4\), and \(\frac{15 - (-27)}{7} = 6\). Combining them according to the operations gives \(8 - 4 - 6 = -2\).

The first fraction simplifies to \(\frac{-2[-27 - 18]}{-6} = \frac{90}{-6} = -15\). The second fraction simplifies to \(\frac{25 - 9^2}{-6 + 2} = \frac{-56}{-4} = 14\). Subtracting gives \(-15 - 14 = -29\).

Simplify inner brackets and powers first: the first numerator is \(-3[8 - 9] + 5 = 8\), so \(\frac{8}{-2} = -4\). The second numerator is \(64 - 2(8) = 48\), so \(\frac{48}{-3} = -16\). Subtracting gives \(-4 - (-16) = 12\).

exercises.name: Word Problems Involving Integers and Exponents

qs.q: A research submarine was at an elevation of -280 m at 8:00 am and rose to -40 m at 12:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in elevation between 8:00 am and 12:00 pm.
qs.s: The time elapsed from 8:00 am to 12:00 pm is 4 hours. The rate of change is [-40 - (-280)] / 4 = 240 / 4 = 60 m/h.

qs.q: The temperature outside a weather station was -35°C at 4:00 am and warmed to 5°C at 2:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in temperature between 4:00 am and 2:00 pm.
qs.s: The time elapsed from 4:00 am to 2:00 pm is 10 hours. The rate of change is [5 - (-35)] / 10 = 40 / 10 = 4°C/h.

qs.q: The temperature in a refrigerated storage unit was 6°C at 11:00 am and dropped to -18°C at 5:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in temperature between 11:00 am and 5:00 pm.
qs.s: The time elapsed from 11:00 am to 5:00 pm is 6 hours. The rate of change is (-18 - 6) / 6 = -24 / 6 = -4°C/h.

qs.q: The temperature was -15°C at 6:00 am and warmed to 9°C at 2:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in temperature between 6:00 am and 2:00 pm.
qs.s: The time elapsed from 6:00 am to 2:00 pm is 8 hours. The rate of change is [9 - (-15)] / 8 = 24 / 8 = 3°C/h.

qs.q: A weather balloon started at an altitude of -30 m in a valley at 8:00 am and ascended to 90 m at 2:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in altitude between 8:00 am and 2:00 pm.
qs.s: The time elapsed from 8:00 am to 2:00 pm is 6 hours. The rate of change is [90 - (-30)] / 6 = 120 / 6 = 20 m/h.

qs.q: A weather station recorded a temperature of -32°C at 4:00 am, -8°C at 10:00 am, and 10°C at 1:00 pm on the same day. How much greater was the rate of change in temperature between 10:00 am and 1:00 pm than between 4:00 am and 10:00 am?
qs.s: The warming rate from 4:00 am to 10:00 am was [-8 - (-32)] / 6 = 4°C/h, and from 10:00 am to 1:00 pm it was [10 - (-8)] / 3 = 6°C/h. The difference between the rates is 6 - 4 = 2°C/h.

qs.q: At 7:00 am, a research submarine was at an elevation of -500 m. From 7:00 am to 11:00 am, it ascended at a rate of 45 m/h. From 11:00 am to 1:00 pm, it descended at a rate of 20 m/h. From 1:00 pm to 3:00 pm, it ascended at a rate of 10 m/h. What was the submarine's overall rate of change in elevation per hour between 7:00 am and 3:00 pm?
qs.s: The total change in elevation over the 8 hours was 4(45) + 2(-20) + 2(10) = 180 - 40 + 20 = 160 m. The overall rate of change was 160 / 8 = 20 m/h.

qs.q: The temperature in an industrial freezer was -14°C at 5:00 am. Due to a power outage, it warmed at a steady rate of 3°C per hour until 11:00 am. Emergency power was then restored, and the freezer cooled at a constant rate until it reached -20°C at 5:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in temperature between 11:00 am and 5:00 pm.
qs.s: At 11:00 am, the temperature was -14 + 3(6) = 4°C. Between 11:00 am and 5:00 pm (6 hours), the rate of change was (-20 - 4) / 6 = -24 / 6 = -4°C/h.

qs.q: A mining elevator was at an elevation of -120 m at 6:00 am. It descended at a rate of 45 m/h for 4 hours, remained stationary for 1 hour, and then ascended at a constant rate until it reached an elevation of -60 m at 3:00 pm the same day. Find the rate of change in elevation during the ascent.
qs.s: At 11:00 am, the elevator was at -120 + 4(-45) = -300 m. Between 11:00 am and 3:00 pm (4 hours), the rate of change during the ascent was [-60 - (-300)] / 4 = 240 / 4 = 60 m/h.

qs.q: On the same winter day, City A had a temperature of -18°C at 2:00 am and warmed to 6°C at 2:00 pm. City B had a temperature of -29°C at 5:00 am and warmed to 11°C at 1:00 pm. How much greater was the rate of warming in City B than in City A, in °C per hour?
qs.s: City A warmed at [6 - (-18)] / 12 = 2°C/h, while City B warmed at [11 - (-29)] / 8 = 5°C/h. The rate of warming in City B was 5 - 2 = 3°C/h greater.

exercises.name: Word Problems Involving Integers and Exponents

qs.q: A single bacterium divides into 2 bacteria every hour. How many bacteria will there be after 8 hours?
qs.s: The population doubles every hour for 8 hours, which is calculated as \(2^8 = 256\) bacteria.

qs.q: A chain message instructs each recipient to forward the email to 4 friends. If 1 person starts the chain by sending it to 4 friends in the first stage, how many people will receive the message in the 5th stage?
qs.s: The number of recipients multiplies by 4 at each stage, so the 5th stage has \(4^5 = 1024\) recipients.

qs.q: In a trivia game, each consecutive correct answer triples your score multiplier, starting from 1. What is the multiplier after answering 5 questions correctly in a row?
qs.s: Tripling the score 5 times in a row is represented by \(3^5 = 243\).

qs.q: A large sheet of paper is folded in half repeatedly. Each fold doubles the number of layers. How many layers thick is the paper after 7 folds?
qs.s: Since the number of layers doubles with each fold, after 7 folds there are \(2^7 = 128\) layers.

qs.q: In a single-elimination tournament, the final round has 2 teams, the semifinals have 4 teams, and each earlier round has twice as many teams as the round after it. How many teams played in the first round if the tournament lasted 6 rounds?
qs.s: The number of teams doubles for each of the 6 rounds, which gives \(2^6 = 64\) teams.

qs.q: Each person has 2 biological parents, 4 grandparents, and so on. What is the total number of ancestors a person has across the 4 most recent generations combined?
qs.s: Calculate the ancestors in each of the 4 generations (\(2^1 = 2\), \(2^2 = 4\), \(2^3 = 8\), \(2^4 = 16\)) and add them together: \(2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 30\).

qs.q: In an academic competition, a team earns \(4^3\) points in Round 1, loses \(2^5\) points in penalties during Round 2, and gains \(3 \cdot 2^3\) bonus points in Round 3. What is the team's final score?
qs.s: Evaluate the exponents to get \(64 - 32 + 3 \cdot 8\), multiply to get \(64 - 32 + 24\), and then compute from left to right: \(32 + 24 = 56\).

qs.q: In a biology experiment, Dish A starts with 3 bacteria that double every hour for 5 hours. Dish B starts with 4 bacteria that triple every hour for 3 hours. What is the total number of bacteria in both dishes combined at the end of this time?
qs.s: Evaluate the exponents first and multiply: Dish A has \(3 \cdot 2^5 = 3 \cdot 32 = 96\) bacteria and Dish B has \(4 \cdot 3^3 = 4 \cdot 27 = 108\) bacteria. Adding them gives \(96 + 108 = 204\).

qs.q: A laboratory culture starts with 5 cells that double in number every hour. After 6 hours, 40 cells are removed for testing. How many cells remain in the culture?
qs.s: Following the order of operations, calculate the total growth first as \(5 \cdot 2^6 = 5 \cdot 64 = 320\), then subtract the removed cells: \(320 - 40 = 280\).

qs.q: A computer virus spreads such that the number of infected computers on Day \(d\) is given by \(3^d\). How many more computers are infected on Day 6 than on Day 4?
qs.s: Evaluate the powers first: \(3^6 = 729\) and \(3^4 = 81\). Then find the difference: \(729 - 81 = 648\).

exercises.name: Word Problems Involving Integers and Exponents

qs.q: Liam had $56 in his checking account. After buying 7 identical movie tickets for his friends, his account balance was -$21. What was the price of each movie ticket?
qs.s: The total amount spent was \(56 - (-\)21) = $77. Dividing by 7 tickets gives $77 \div 7 = $11 per ticket.

qs.q: Elena started a trivia game with 45 points. After answering 9 questions incorrectly in a penalty round, her score was -18 points. If each incorrect answer had the same penalty, how many points were deducted for each incorrect answer?
qs.s: The total points lost was 45 - (-18) = 63 points. Dividing by 9 questions gives a deduction of 63 \div 9 = 7 points per incorrect answer.

qs.q: At 6:00 p.m., the temperature outside was 18°C. Over the next 6 hours, the temperature dropped at a constant rate to -12°C. By how many degrees Celsius did the temperature drop each hour?
qs.s: The total decrease in temperature was 18 - (-12) = 30°C. Dividing by 6 hours gives an average drop of 30 \div 6 = 5°C per hour.

qs.q: A hiker started on a trail at 85 meters above sea level. After descending into a canyon across 5 equal stages, the hiker's elevation was -40 meters. How many meters did the hiker descend in each stage?
qs.s: The total descent was 85 - (-40) = 125 meters. Dividing by 5 stages gives a descent of 125 \div 5 = 25 meters per stage.

qs.q: Marcus had $84 in his checking account. After paying for 12 identical board games for a youth club, his account balance was -$36. What was the cost of each board game?
qs.s: The total amount spent was \(84 - (-\)36) = $120. Dividing by the 12 board games gives $120 \div 12 = $10 per game.

qs.q: A small retailer had $240 in store credit. After receiving an additional promotional credit of $120, the retailer placed an order for 12 identical lamps. The order left the account with a balance of -$72. What was the price of each lamp?
qs.s: The total credit before purchasing was $240 + $120 = $360. The total spent on the lamps was \(360 - (-\)72) = $432, so each lamp cost $432 \div 12 = $36.

qs.q: In a science lab, a chemical solution starts at a temperature of \(4^3\) °C. It is placed into a deep freezer where its temperature drops at a constant rate for \(2^3\) minutes, reaching a final temperature of -32°C. By how many degrees Celsius did the temperature drop each minute?
qs.s: The initial temperature is \(4^3 = 64\)°C and the time is \(2^3 = 8\) minutes. The total drop is 64 - (-32) = 96°C, giving an average drop of 96 \div 8 = 12°C per minute.

qs.q: A school club had $360 in its account. It spent \(3^2 \times 20\) dollars on supplies for a fundraiser, and then purchased 12 identical gift baskets. After these expenses, the club's account balance was -$60. What was the cost of each gift basket?
qs.s: The club spent $3^2 \times 20 = 9 \times 20 = $180 on supplies, leaving $360 - $180 = $180. The total spent on the baskets was \(180 - (-\)60) = $240, so each gift basket cost $240 \div 12 = $20.

qs.q: A contestant in a game competition starts with 120 points. During the first round, she earns 30 points in each of 4 challenges. In the second round, she commits 8 identical infractions, leaving her with a final score of -80 points. How many points were deducted for each infraction?
qs.s: Her score before the infractions was 120 + 4(30) = 240 points. The total deducted was 240 - (-80) = 320 points, so each infraction resulted in a deduction of 320 \div 8 = 40 points.

qs.q: A research probe begins at an elevation of \(-4^2\) meters relative to sea level. A crane lifts it up by \(2^6\) meters, and then lowers it into a deep marine trench in 6 equal stages. If the probe's final elevation is -24 meters, how many meters did it descend during each stage?
qs.s: The elevation after being lifted is \(-4^2 + 2^6 = -16 + 64 = 48\) meters. The total descent to -24 meters is 48 - (-24) = 72 meters, so it descended 72 \div 6 = 12 meters per stage.

exercises.name: Word Problems Involving Integers and Exponents

qs.q: A mining elevator descended into a shaft for 22 minutes to reach the bottom. Its rate of descent was \(-15\text{ m/min}\). After every 3 minutes of descent, it stopped for 1 minute for a safety check. How deep was the bottom of the shaft?
qs.s: In 22 minutes, there are 5 full 4-minute cycles (3 min descent + 1 min stop) plus 2 minutes of descent, giving \(5(3) + 2 = 17\) minutes of descending. The depth is \(17\text{ min} \times 15\text{ m/min} = 255\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rock climber took 34 minutes to rappel down a vertical cliff face. His rate of descent was \(-7\text{ m/min}\). After every 6 minutes of descending, he paused for 1 minute to check his gear. How tall was the cliff face?
qs.s: In 34 minutes, there are 4 full 7-minute cycles (6 min descent + 1 min pause) plus 6 minutes of descent, giving \(4(6) + 6 = 30\) minutes of descending. The cliff face is \(30\text{ min} \times 7\text{ m/min} = 210\text{ m}\) tall.

qs.q: A deep-sea research probe took 29 minutes to reach the seabed. Its rate of descent was \(-12\text{ m/min}\). After every 5 minutes of descending, it stopped for 1 minute to take water samples. How deep was the seabed?
qs.s: In 29 minutes, there are 4 full 6-minute cycles (5 min descent + 1 min stop) plus 5 minutes of descent, giving \(4(5) + 5 = 25\) minutes of descending. The seabed depth is \(25\text{ min} \times 12\text{ m/min} = 300\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A thermal drill took 19 minutes to reach an underground aquifer. Its rate of penetration was \(-6\text{ m/min}\). After every 4 minutes of drilling, the motor was stopped for 1 minute to cool down. What was the depth of the aquifer?
qs.s: In 19 minutes, there are 3 full 5-minute cycles (4 min drilling + 1 min pause) plus 4 minutes of drilling, giving \(3(4) + 4 = 16\) minutes of drilling. The depth of the aquifer is \(16\text{ min} \times 6\text{ m/min} = 96\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A submarine took 22 minutes to descend from the surface to an underwater research base. Its rate of descent was \(-9\text{ m/min}\). After every 4 minutes of descent, it paused for 2 minutes to adjust ballast. How deep was the research base?
qs.s: In 22 minutes, there are 3 full 6-minute cycles (4 min descent + 2 min pause) plus 4 minutes of descent, giving \(3(4) + 4 = 16\) minutes of descending. The depth is \(16\text{ min} \times 9\text{ m/min} = 144\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A deep-sea submersible descended from the surface to an ocean trench at a depth of \(-720\text{ m}\). Its rate of descent was \(-16\text{ m/min}\). After every 6 minutes of descent, it paused for 2 minutes to scan the terrain. What was the total elapsed time, in minutes, from when the submersible left the surface until it reached the trench?
qs.s: Descending \(720\text{ m}\) requires \(720 \div 16 = 45\) minutes of descent. In 45 minutes of movement, there are \(45 \div 6 = 7\) full pauses before reaching the trench, so the total time is \(45 + 7(2) = 45 + 14 = 59\text{ minutes}\).

qs.q: A subterranean exploration drill starts at a depth of \(-45\text{ m}\) below ground. It operates for 58 minutes with a rate of descent of \(-14\text{ m/min}\). After every 7 minutes of drilling, it pauses for 3 minutes to clear debris. How deep below ground level is the drill at the end of the 58 minutes?
qs.s: In 58 minutes, there are 5 full 10-minute cycles plus an 8-minute remainder (7 min drilling and 1 min pause), totaling \(5(7) + 7 = 42\) minutes of drilling. The final depth is \(45 + 42(14) = 45 + 588 = 633\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A deep-sea diver begins at the surface and descends at a rate of \(-6\text{ m/min}\) for a total elapsed time of 32 minutes, pausing for 1 minute after every 5 minutes of descent. From that point, she ascends toward the surface at a rate of \(+4\text{ m/min}\) for 15 minutes without pausing. How deep is she at the end of the dive?
qs.s: In 32 minutes, there are 5 full 6-minute cycles plus 2 minutes of descent, giving \(5(5) + 2 = 27\) minutes descending to a depth of \(27 \times 6 = 162\text{ m}\). Ascending for 15 minutes reduces the depth by \(15 \times 4 = 60\text{ m}\), leaving her at \(162 - 60 = 102\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A cryogenic freezer cools a solution currently at \(15^\circ\text{C}\). The freezer lowers the temperature at a rate of \(-3^\circ\text{C/min}\). After every 6 minutes of cooling, the freezer pauses for 2 minutes to stabilize. The cooling process runs for 38 minutes in total. Finally, a coolant is added that drops the temperature by an additional \(2^4{}^\circ\text{C}\). What is the final temperature of the solution?
qs.s: In 38 minutes, there are 4 full 8-minute cycles plus 6 minutes of cooling, giving \(4(6) + 6 = 30\) minutes of cooling. The final temperature is \(15 + 30(-3) - 2^4 = 15 - 90 - 16 = -91^\circ\text{C}\).

qs.q: A weather balloon is released from a research station at an elevation of \(2 \times 10^3\text{ m}\) above sea level. It ascends for 43 minutes at a rate of \(15\text{ m/min}\). After every 8 minutes of ascent, it pauses for 2 minutes to transmit data. What is the balloon's final elevation above sea level?
qs.s: In 43 minutes, there are 4 full 10-minute cycles plus 3 minutes of ascent, giving \(4(8) + 3 = 35\) minutes of ascending. The final elevation is \(2 \times 10^3 + 35(15) = 2000 + 525 = 2525\text{ m}\).

exercises.name: Find prism dimension from surface area

qs.q: The total surface area of a cube is \(216\text{ cm}^2\). What is the length of each edge of the cube?
qs.s: Since \(SA = 6s^2\), setting \(6s^2 = 216\) gives \(s^2 = 36\). Taking the square root gives an edge length of \(s = 6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A cube-shaped box has a total surface area of \(54\text{ cm}^2\). What is the side length of the box?
qs.s: Using the formula \(SA = 6s^2\), we have \(6s^2 = 54\), which simplifies to \(s^2 = 9\). Taking the square root yields \(s = 3\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: If the surface area of a cube is \(96\text{ cm}^2\), what is the length of each side of the cube?
qs.s: The surface area of a cube is \(SA = 6s^2\), so \(6s^2 = 96\). Dividing by 6 gives \(s^2 = 16\), and taking the square root gives \(s = 4\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: If the total surface area of a cube is \(294\text{ m}^2\), what is the length of each edge of the cube?
qs.s: Divide the surface area by 6 to find the area of one face: \(s^2 = 294 / 6 = 49\). Taking the square root gives an edge length of \(s = 7\text{ m}\).

qs.q: If the surface area of a cube is \(384\text{ mm}^2\), what is the length of each side of the cube?
qs.s: Divide the surface area by 6 to find \(s^2 = 384 / 6 = 64\). Taking the square root gives a side length of \(s = 8\text{ mm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base with edge lengths of \(7\text{ cm}\). If the total surface area of the prism is \(378\text{ cm}^2\), what is the height of the prism?
qs.s: The two square bases contribute \(2(7^2) = 98\text{ cm}^2\), leaving \(378 - 98 = 280\text{ cm}^2\) for the four lateral faces. Dividing by the four face widths gives \(h = 280 / (4 \times 7) = 10\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base, and its height is twice the side length of the base. If the total surface area of the prism is \(360\text{ cm}^2\), what is the side length of the base?
qs.s: Let \(s\) be the side length of the base, so the height is \(2s\). The total surface area is \(2(s^2) + 4(s \times 2s) = 10s^2 = 360\), which simplifies to \(s^2 = 36\), giving \(s = 6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The total surface area of a cube is \(37.5\text{ cm}^2\). What is the length of each edge of the cube?
qs.s: Using \(SA = 6s^2\), dividing by 6 gives \(s^2 = 37.5 / 6 = 6.25\). Taking the square root gives an edge length of \(s = 2.5\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length of \(8\text{ cm}\), a width of \(5\text{ cm}\), and a total surface area of \(158\text{ cm}^2\). What is the height of the prism?
qs.s: The top and bottom faces have a combined area of \(2(8 \times 5) = 80\text{ cm}^2\), leaving \(158 - 80 = 78\text{ cm}^2\) for the lateral faces. Dividing by the base perimeter gives \(h = 78 / 2(8 + 5) = 78 / 26 = 3\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: If the total surface area of a cube is \(1176\text{ cm}^2\), what is the length of each side of the cube?
qs.s: Divide the total surface area by 6 to find the area of one face: \(s^2 = 1176 / 6 = 196\). Taking the square root yields \(s = 14\text{ cm}\).

exercises.name: Surface area from edge lengths or dimension relations

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a width twice its height, and a length five times its height. If the height is 3 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The dimensions are height = 3 cm, width = 2 × 3 = 6 cm, and length = 5 × 3 = 15 cm. The surface area is 2(15 × 6 + 15 × 3 + 6 × 3) = 2(90 + 45 + 18) = 306 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length twice its width, and a height half its width. If the width is 8 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The dimensions are width = 8 cm, length = 2 × 8 = 16 cm, and height = 8 / 2 = 4 cm. The surface area is 2(16 × 8 + 16 × 4 + 8 × 4) = 2(128 + 64 + 32) = 448 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a height three times its length, and a width that is one-third of its length. If the length is 9 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The dimensions are length = 9 cm, height = 3 × 9 = 27 cm, and width = 9 / 3 = 3 cm. The surface area is 2(9 × 3 + 9 × 27 + 3 × 27) = 2(27 + 243 + 81) = 702 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length of 10 cm. Its width is half its length, and its height is 2 cm less than its width. What is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The dimensions are length = 10 cm, width = 10 / 2 = 5 cm, and height = 5 - 2 = 3 cm. The surface area is 2(10 × 5 + 10 × 3 + 5 × 3) = 2(50 + 30 + 15) = 190 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length three times its width, and a height equal to twice its width. If the width is 4 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The dimensions are width = 4 cm, length = 3 × 4 = 12 cm, and height = 2 × 4 = 8 cm. The surface area is 2(12 × 4 + 12 × 8 + 4 × 8) = 2(48 + 96 + 32) = 352 cm².

qs.q: The sum of the lengths of all 12 edges of a rectangular prism is 100 cm. The length is three times the width, and the height is 5 cm greater than the width. What is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: Since 4(l + w + h) = 100, we have l + w + h = 25. Substituting l = 3w and h = w + 5 gives 5w + 5 = 25, so w = 4 cm, l = 12 cm, and h = 9 cm; thus, surface area = 2(12 × 4 + 12 × 9 + 4 × 9) = 384 cm².

qs.q: An open-top rectangular box (with no top face) has a length of 20 cm. Its width is 3/5 of its length, and its height is half of its width. What is the total outside surface area of the box?
qs.s: The dimensions are length = 20 cm, width = 12 cm, and height = 6 cm. Since there is no top face, the surface area is lw + 2lh + 2wh = (20 × 12) + 2(20 × 6) + 2(12 × 6) = 240 + 240 + 144 = 624 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base. The height of the prism is 3 cm more than twice the side length of the base. If the perimeter of the base is 24 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The base edge is 24 / 4 = 6 cm, and the height is 2(6) + 3 = 15 cm. The surface area is 2(6 × 6) + 4(6 × 15) = 72 + 360 = 432 cm².

qs.q: Two identical rectangular prisms, each with a length of 15 cm, a width that is one-third of the length, and a height 2 cm greater than the width, are glued together along their largest faces to form a new rectangular prism. What is the surface area of the new prism?
qs.s: Each prism has dimensions 15 cm by 5 cm by 7 cm, with the largest face having an area of 15 × 7 = 105 cm². Joining them doubles the 5 cm dimension to 10 cm, giving a surface area of 2(15 × 7 + 15 × 10 + 7 × 10) = 650 cm².

qs.q: A cube has an edge length of 12 cm. A rectangular prism has a width equal to half the cube's edge, a length three times its own width, and a height 2 cm less than the cube's edge. What is the difference between the surface area of the cube and the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: The cube has surface area 6(12²) = 864 cm². The prism has dimensions w = 6 cm, l = 18 cm, and h = 10 cm, with surface area 2(18 × 6 + 18 × 10 + 6 × 10) = 696 cm², so the difference is 864 - 696 = 168 cm².

exercises.name: Surface area from edge lengths or dimension relations

qs.q: If the sum of the edges of a cube is 48 cm, what is the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: A cube has 12 equal edges, so each edge length is 48 ÷ 12 = 4 cm. The surface area is 6 × 4² = 6 × 16 = 96 cm².

qs.q: If the sum of the edges of a cube is 72 cm, what is the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: A cube has 12 equal edges, so each edge length is 72 ÷ 12 = 6 cm. The surface area is 6 × 6² = 6 × 36 = 216 cm².

qs.q: If the sum of the edges of a cube is 60 cm, what is the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: A cube has 12 equal edges, so each edge length is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cm. The surface area is 6 × 5² = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

qs.q: If the sum of the edges of a cube is 96 cm, what is the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: A cube has 12 equal edges, so each edge length is 96 ÷ 12 = 8 cm. The surface area is 6 × 8² = 6 × 64 = 384 cm².

qs.q: If the sum of the edges of a cube is 108 cm, what is the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: A cube has 12 equal edges, so each edge length is 108 ÷ 12 = 9 cm. The surface area is 6 × 9² = 6 × 81 = 486 cm².

qs.q: The sum of all 12 edges of a rectangular prism is 84 cm. The length of the prism is twice its height, and its width is 6 cm. What is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: Since 4(l + w + h) = 84, l + w + h = 21 cm, so 2h + 6 + h = 21 gives 3h = 15, meaning h = 5 cm and l = 10 cm. The surface area is 2(10 × 6 + 10 × 5 + 6 × 5) = 2(60 + 50 + 30) = 280 cm².

qs.q: A cube has a sum of edges equal to 144 cm. A second cube has an edge length that is 3 cm longer than the edge length of the first cube. What is the surface area of the second cube?
qs.s: The first cube has edge length 144 ÷ 12 = 12 cm, so the second cube has edge length 12 + 3 = 15 cm. The surface area of the second cube is 6 × 15² = 6 × 225 = 1350 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length of 8 cm and a width of 5 cm. If the sum of all 12 edges is 68 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
The length, width, and height of a rectangular prism are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. If the sum of all 12 edges of the prism is 72 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The sum of all edges is 4(x + 2x + 3x) = 24x = 72 cm, so x = 3 cm. The dimensions are 3 cm, 6 cm, and 9 cm, giving a surface area of 2(3 × 6 + 3 × 9 + 6 × 9) = 2(18 + 27 + 54) = 198 cm².

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base, and its height is twice the side length of the base. If the sum of all 12 edges of the prism is 64 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: The sum of the edges is 8s + 4(2s) = 16s = 64 cm, giving base edge s = 4 cm and height h = 8 cm. The surface area is 2(4 × 4) + 4(4 × 8) = 32 + 128 = 160 cm².

exercises.name: Surface area from edge lengths or dimension relations

qs.q: A cube has edges such that the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 84 cm. What is the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: A cube has 12 equal edges, so each edge length is \(84 \div 12 = 7\) cm. The surface area is \(6 \times 7^2 = 6 \times 49 = 294\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base. The side length of the square base is twice the height of the prism. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 60 cm, what is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: Let the height be \(h\) cm, so the base edge is \(2h\) cm. The sum of the edges is \(8(2h) + 4h = 20h = 60\), which gives \(h = 3\) cm and base edge \(6\) cm. The surface area is \(2(6^2) + 4(6 \times 3) = 72 + 72 = 144\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base and a height that is three times the side length of the base. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 80 cm, what is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: Let the side length of the base be \(x\) cm, so the height is \(3x\) cm. The sum of the edges is \(8x + 4(3x) = 20x = 80\), so \(x = 4\) cm and the height is \(12\) cm. The surface area is \(2(4^2) + 4(4 \times 12) = 32 + 192 = 224\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base, and its height is 4 times the side length of its base. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 96 cm, what is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: Let the base side length be \(x\) cm and height be \(4x\) cm; the sum of edges is \(8x + 4(4x) = 24x = 96\), giving \(x = 4\) cm and height \(16\) cm. The surface area is \(2(4^2) + 4(4 \times 16) = 32 + 256 = 288\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base and a height that is 5 times the side length of the base. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 56 cm, what is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: Let the base side length be \(x\) cm, so the height is \(5x\) cm. The sum of the edges is \(8x + 4(5x) = 28x = 56\), giving \(x = 2\) cm and height \(10\) cm. The surface area is \(2(2^2) + 4(2 \times 10) = 8 + 80 = 88\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has dimensions in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 112 cm, what is the surface area of the prism?
qs.s: Let the dimensions be \(x\), \(2x\), and \(4x\). The sum of the edges is \(4(x + 2x + 4x) = 28x = 112\), so \(x = 4\) cm and the dimensions are \(4\) cm, \(8\) cm, and \(16\) cm. The surface area is \(2(4 \times 8 + 4 \times 16 + 8 \times 16) = 2(32 + 64 + 128) = 448\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length that is twice its width, and a height that is three times its width. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 168 cm, what is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: Let the width be \(w\), so length is \(2w\) and height is \(3w\). The sum of all 12 edges is \(4(w + 2w + 3w) = 24w = 168\), giving \(w = 7\) cm, \(l = 14\) cm, and \(h = 21\) cm. The surface area is \(2(14 \times 7 + 14 \times 21 + 7 \times 21) = 2(98 + 294 + 147) = 1078\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base and a height that is three times the side length of the base. If the total surface area of the prism is 350 cm², what is the sum of the lengths of all its edges?
qs.s: Let the base side length be \(x\) cm and height be \(3x\) cm. The surface area is \(2(x^2) + 4(x \times 3x) = 14x^2 = 350\), so \(x^2 = 25\) and \(x = 5\) cm. The sum of the edges is \(8(5) + 4(15) = 40 + 60 = 100\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: An open-top rectangular box has a square base. The height of the box is 3 times the side length of the base. If the sum of the lengths of all 12 of its edges is 120 cm, what is the outside surface area of the box?
qs.s: Let the base edge be \(x\) cm and height be \(3x\) cm. The sum of the 12 edges is \(8x + 4(3x) = 20x = 120\), giving \(x = 6\) cm and height \(18\) cm. Since the top is open, the outside surface area is \(x^2 + 4(x \times 3x) = 6^2 + 4(6 \times 18) = 36 + 432 = 468\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base. Its height is 6 cm longer than the side length of the square base. If the sum of the lengths of all its edges is 96 cm, what is the surface area of the rectangular prism?
qs.s: Let the base side length be \(x\) cm, so the height is \(x + 6\) cm. The sum of the edges is \(8x + 4(x + 6) = 12x + 24 = 96\), giving \(x = 6\) cm and height \(12\) cm. The surface area is \(2(6^2) + 4(6 \times 12) = 72 + 288 = 360\text{ cm}^2\).

exercises.name: Find prism dimension from surface area

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length three times the width, and a height half the width. If the surface area is 360 cm², what is the width?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(3w \times w + 3w \times 0.5w + w \times 0.5w) = 10w^2\). Setting \(10w^2 = 360\) gives \(w^2 = 36\), so the width is \(6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length twice the width, and a height half the width. If the surface area is 112 cm², what is the width?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(2w \times w + 2w \times 0.5w + w \times 0.5w) = 7w^2\). Setting \(7w^2 = 112\) gives \(w^2 = 16\), so the width is \(4\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length three times the width, and a height equal to the width. If the surface area is 126 cm², what is the width?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(3w \times w + 3w \times w + w \times w) = 14w^2\). Setting \(14w^2 = 126\) gives \(w^2 = 9\), so the width is \(3\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length twice the width, and a height equal to the width. If the surface area is 250 cm², what is the width?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(2w \times w + 2w \times w + w \times w) = 10w^2\). Setting \(10w^2 = 250\) gives \(w^2 = 25\), so the width is \(5\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length three times the width, and a height twice the width. If the surface area is 88 cm², what is the width?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(3w \times w + 3w \times 2w + w \times 2w) = 22w^2\). Setting \(22w^2 = 88\) gives \(w^2 = 4\), so the width is \(2\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a width four times its height, and a length six times its height. If the surface area is 1700 cm², what is the length of the prism?
qs.s: The surface area in terms of height \(h\) is \(2(24h^2 + 6h^2 + 4h^2) = 68h^2\). Setting \(68h^2 = 1700\) yields \(h^2 = 25\), so \(h = 5\text{ cm}\) and the length is \(6 \times 5 = 30\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length 2.5 times its width, and a height 1.5 times its width. If the surface area is 248 cm², what is the height of the prism?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(2.5w^2 + 3.75w^2 + 1.5w^2) = 15.5w^2\). Setting \(15.5w^2 = 248\) gives \(w^2 = 16\) so \(w = 4\text{ cm}\), making the height \(1.5 \times 4 = 6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length twice its width, and a height three times its length. If the surface area is 1440 cm², what is the height of the prism?
qs.s: Since \(l = 2w\) and \(h = 3(2w) = 6w\), the surface area is \(2(2w^2 + 12w^2 + 6w^2) = 40w^2\). Setting \(40w^2 = 1440\) yields \(w = 6\text{ cm}\), so the height is \(6 \times 6 = 36\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length three times its width, and a height twice its width. If the surface area is 352 cm², what is the sum of the lengths of all twelve edges?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(3w^2 + 6w^2 + 2w^2) = 22w^2 = 352\), giving \(w^2 = 16\) and \(w = 4\text{ cm}\). The sum of all twelve edges is \(4(l + w + h) = 4(3w + w + 2w) = 24w = 24(4) = 96\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length three times its width, and a height four times its width. If the surface area is 608 cm², what is the length of the prism?
qs.s: The surface area is \(2(3w^2 + 12w^2 + 4w^2) = 38w^2 = 608\), which gives \(w^2 = 16\) and \(w = 4\text{ cm}\). The length is \(3 \times 4 = 12\text{ cm}\).

exercises.name: Effect of scaling dimensions on surface area

qs.q: If the linear dimensions of a triangular prism are all multiplied by 5, what happens to the total surface area?
qs.s: Scaling all dimensions of a prism by 5 multiplies the area of every triangular and rectangular face by \(5^2 = 25\). As a result, the total surface area is multiplied by 25.

qs.q: If all the edge lengths of a box are divided by 3, what happens to the surface area?
qs.s: Dividing each dimension by 3 multiplies the linear dimensions by \(\frac{1}{3}\), which scales the area of each face by \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{9}\). Hence, the total surface area is divided by 9.

qs.q: If all the edges of a box are halved in length, what happens to the surface area?
qs.s: Halving every edge scales the dimensions by a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\), which scales the area of each face by \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\). Therefore, the surface area is divided by 4.

qs.q: If the edges of a box are tripled in length, what happens to the surface area?
qs.s: Because surface area is a two-dimensional measure, scaling every linear dimension by a factor of 3 multiplies the area of each face by \(3^2 = 9\). Therefore, the total surface area is multiplied by 9.

qs.q: If each edge of a rectangular prism is quadrupled in length, what happens to its surface area?
qs.s: Multiplying each edge by 4 scales the area of each rectangular face by \(4^2 = 16\). Thus, the total surface area is multiplied by 16.

qs.q: When all edge lengths of a box are multiplied by the same factor, its total surface area increases from \(45\text{ cm}^2\) to \(405\text{ cm}^2\). By what factor were the edge lengths multiplied?
qs.s: The surface area increases by a factor of \(\frac{405}{45} = 9\). Since the surface area scale factor is the square of the linear scale factor, the edge lengths were multiplied by \(\sqrt{9} = 3\).

qs.q: A cube has an edge length of \(3\text{ cm}\). If each edge length is doubled, by how much does the total surface area increase?
qs.s: The original surface area is \(6 \times 3^2 = 54\text{ cm}^2\), and the new surface area is \(54 \times 2^2 = 216\text{ cm}^2\). The increase in surface area is \(216 - 54 = 162\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length of \(6\text{ cm}\), a width of \(3\text{ cm}\), and a height of \(2\text{ cm}\). If all of its edge lengths are doubled, what is the total surface area of the enlarged prism?
qs.s: The original surface area is \(2(6 \times 3 + 6 \times 2 + 3 \times 2) = 2(18 + 12 + 6) = 72\text{ cm}^2\). Doubling all edge lengths multiplies the surface area by \(2^2 = 4\), giving \(72 \times 4 = 288\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a total surface area of \(160\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its edges are multiplied by \(\frac{3}{2}\), what is the new total surface area?
qs.s: Multiplying the edge lengths by \(\frac{3}{2}\) scales the surface area by \(\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{4}\). The new surface area is \(160 \times \frac{9}{4} = 360\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A triangular prism has a total surface area of \(840\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its dimensions are reduced to \(\frac{1}{2}\) of their original lengths, what is the total surface area of the smaller prism?
qs.s: Scaling all linear dimensions by \(\frac{1}{2}\) multiplies the total surface area by \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\). The new surface area is \(840 \times \frac{1}{4} = 210\text{ cm}^2\).

exercises.name: Effect of scaling dimensions on surface area

qs.q: If all the edges of a box are doubled in length, what happens to the surface area?
qs.s: Surface area is proportional to the square of the linear dimensions. When the edges are doubled, the surface area is multiplied by \(2^2 = 4\).

qs.q: If the edges of a cube are multiplied by 5, what happens to the surface area of the cube?
qs.s: Because surface area depends on the product of two linear dimensions, multiplying each edge length by 5 multiplies the surface area by \(5^2 = 25\).

qs.q: If all linear dimensions of a right triangular prism are multiplied by 6, what happens to its surface area?
qs.s: Scaling all linear dimensions of a prism by a factor of 6 scales the total surface area by \(6^2 = 36\).

qs.q: If all dimensions of a rectangular prism are quadrupled, what happens to its total surface area?
qs.s: Surface area scales with the square of the linear dimensions. When the dimensions are quadrupled, the surface area is multiplied by \(4^2 = 16\).

qs.q: If each edge of a box is reduced to half its original length, what happens to the surface area?
qs.s: Reducing the edge lengths to half means scaling by a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\). The surface area is therefore multiplied by \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a surface area of \(120\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its edges are multiplied by a scale factor of \(\frac{3}{2}\), what is the surface area of the new prism?
qs.s: Multiplying each edge by \(\frac{3}{2}\) multiplies the surface area by \(\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{4}\). The new surface area is \(120 \times \frac{9}{4} = 270\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A cube has an edge length of \(5\text{ cm}\). If each of its edges is tripled in length, by how much does its surface area increase?
qs.s: The original surface area is \(6 \times 5^2 = 150\text{ cm}^2\), and tripling the edges multiplies the area by \(3^2 = 9\) to give \(1350\text{ cm}^2\). The increase in surface area is \(1350 - 150 = 1200\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: The surface area of a prism increases from \(45\text{ cm}^2\) to \(720\text{ cm}^2\) when all of its linear dimensions are multiplied by the same factor \(k\). What is the value of \(k\)?
qs.s: The surface area increases by a factor of \(\frac{720}{45} = 16\). Since surface area scales by \(k^2\), we have \(k^2 = 16\), which gives \(k = 4\).

qs.q: A right triangular prism has a base with legs \(6\text{ cm}\) and \(8\text{ cm}\) (hypotenuse \(10\text{ cm}\)) and a length of \(5\text{ cm}\). If all of its dimensions are halved, what is the surface area of the smaller prism?
qs.s: The original surface area is \(2\left(\frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8\right) + (6 + 8 + 10) \times 5 = 48 + 120 = 168\text{ cm}^2\). Halving the dimensions multiplies the surface area by \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\), giving \(168 \times \frac{1}{4} = 42\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular box has a length of \(6\text{ cm}\), a width of \(4\text{ cm}\), and a height of \(3\text{ cm}\). If all of its edges are doubled in length, what is the surface area of the new box?
qs.s: The original surface area is \(2(6 \times 4 + 6 \times 3 + 4 \times 3) = 108\text{ cm}^2\). Doubling all dimensions multiplies the surface area by \(2^2 = 4\), so the new surface area is \(108 \times 4 = 432\text{ cm}^2\).

exercises.name: Effect of scaling dimensions on surface area

qs.q: A prism has a surface area of \(45\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its linear dimensions are doubled, what is the new surface area?
qs.s: Doubling the linear dimensions increases the surface area by a factor of \(2^2 = 4\). Thus, the new surface area is \(45 \times 4 = 180\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: In general, if each dimension of a prism is multiplied by a factor of \(k\), by what factor is the total surface area multiplied?
qs.s: Because surface area is a two-dimensional measurement involving products of pairs of dimensions, scaling all dimensions by \(k\) multiplies the surface area by \(k \times k = k^2\).

qs.q: If all linear dimensions of a prism are multiplied by \(3\), by what factor does the total surface area increase?
qs.s: Since surface area is proportional to the square of linear dimensions, multiplying each dimension by \(3\) increases the surface area by a factor of \(3^2 = 9\).

qs.q: A triangular prism has an original surface area of \(32\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its dimensions are multiplied by \(5\), what is its new surface area?
qs.s: Multiplying all dimensions by \(5\) scales the surface area by \(5^2 = 25\). The new surface area is \(32 \times 25 = 800\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: If each dimension of a rectangular prism is scaled by a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\), by what factor is its total surface area scaled?
qs.s: Scaling the linear dimensions by \(\frac{1}{2}\) scales the surface area by \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\).

qs.q: Two similar rectangular prisms, Prism A and Prism B, have linear dimensions in the ratio \(1 : 3\), meaning each dimension of Prism B is \(3\) times the corresponding dimension of Prism A. If the total surface area of Prism B is \(432\text{ cm}^2\), what is the total surface area of Prism A?
qs.s: Because each dimension of Prism B is \(3\) times that of Prism A, the surface area of Prism B is \(3^2 = 9\) times that of Prism A. Thus, the surface area of Prism A is \(\frac{432}{9} = 48\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: The surface area of a prism is \(48\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its linear dimensions are enlarged by a scale factor of \(k\), the new surface area is \(1200\text{ cm}^2\). What is the value of \(k\)?
qs.s: The surface area is scaled by \(k^2\), so \(k^2 = \frac{1200}{48} = 25\). Taking the square root gives \(k = 5\).

qs.q: A triangular prism has an original surface area of \(120\text{ cm}^2\). If all of its linear dimensions are multiplied by \(4\), by how much does its surface area increase?
qs.s: Multiplying the dimensions by \(4\) multiplies the surface area by \(4^2 = 16\), giving a new surface area of \(120 \times 16 = 1920\text{ cm}^2\). The increase is \(1920 - 120 = 1800\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length of \(5\text{ cm}\), a width of \(8\text{ cm}\), and a height of \(10\text{ cm}\). If all of its dimensions are scaled by a factor of \(\frac{3}{2}\), what is the total surface area of the enlarged prism?
qs.s: The original surface area is \(2(5\times 8 + 5\times 10 + 8\times 10) = 340\text{ cm}^2\). Scaling each dimension by \(\frac{3}{2}\) multiplies the surface area by \(\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{4}\), yielding \(340 \times \frac{9}{4} = 765\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: If all linear dimensions of a prism are scaled by a factor of \(\frac{3a}{2}\), by what factor is the surface area of the prism multiplied?
qs.s: Scaling the linear dimensions of a prism by a factor of \(\frac{3a}{2}\) scales the surface area by the square of that factor, which is \(\left(\frac{3a}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{9a^2}{4}\).

qs.s: Convert \(1\frac{1}{7}\) to \(\frac{8}{7}\) and multiply the dimensions: \(V = \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{8}{7} = \frac{360}{420} = \frac{6}{7}\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the volume of a rectangular solid with the given dimensions: \(1\frac{1}{3}\text{ ft}, 1\frac{1}{2}\text{ ft}, 2\frac{1}{4}\text{ ft}\).
qs.s: Convert each dimension to an improper fraction: \(\frac{4}{3}\), \(\frac{3}{2}\), and \(\frac{9}{4}\). Multiply them together: \(V = \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{9}{4} = \frac{9}{2}\text{ ft}^3\).

exercises.name: Solve for prism dimensions using base area and height

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 8\text{ cm}^2\), \(h = 7\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute \(B = 8\text{ cm}^2\) and \(h = 7\text{ cm}\) to find \(V = 8 \times 7 = 56\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 72\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 8\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{72}{8} = 9\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 60\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 5\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{60}{5} = 12\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 42\text{ cm}^3\), \(h = 6\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{42}{6} = 7\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 11\text{ cm}^2\), \(h = 4\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute \(B = 11\text{ cm}^2\) and \(h = 4\text{ cm}\) to find \(V = 11 \times 4 = 44\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 14.5\text{ cm}^2\), \(h = 8.6\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute \(B = 14.5\text{ cm}^2\) and \(h = 8.6\text{ cm}\) to find \(V = 14.5 \times 8.6 = 124.7\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 7\frac{1}{2}\text{ cm}^2\), \(h = 3\frac{1}{5}\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions: \(B = \frac{15}{2}\text{ cm}^2\) and \(h = \frac{16}{5}\text{ cm}\). Using \(V = Bh\), calculate \(V = \frac{15}{2} \times \frac{16}{5} = \frac{240}{10} = 24\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 1512\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 56\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{1512}{56} = 27\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 178.2\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 5.4\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{178.2}{5.4} = 33\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 135\text{ cm}^2\), \(h = 24\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute \(B = 135\text{ cm}^2\) and \(h = 24\text{ cm}\) to find \(V = 135 \times 24 = 3240\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 15\text{ cm}^2\), \(h = 6\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(V = 15 \times 6 = 90\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 63\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 9\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(63 = 9h\). Divide both sides by \(9\) to find \(h = 7\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 84\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 7\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(84 = B \times 7\). Divide both sides by \(7\) to find \(B = 12\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 75\text{ ft}^3\), \(h = 5\text{ ft}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(75 = B \times 5\). Divide both sides by \(5\) to find \(B = 15\text{ ft}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 48\text{ in.}^3\), \(B = 8\text{ in.}^2\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(48 = 8h\). Divide both sides by \(8\) to find \(h = 6\text{ in.}\)

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 1728\text{ cm}^3\), \(h = 16\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(1728 = B \times 16\). Divide both sides by \(16\) to find \(B = 108\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 8\frac{1}{4}\text{ ft}^2\), \(h = 3\frac{1}{3}\text{ ft}\).
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and multiply using \(V = Bh\): \(V = \frac{33}{4} \times \frac{10}{3} = \frac{55}{2} = 27\frac{1}{2}\text{ ft}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 31\frac{1}{2}\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 4\frac{2}{3}\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Convert to improper fractions and solve for \(B\) using \(B = \frac{V}{h}\): \(B = \frac{63}{2} \div \frac{14}{3} = \frac{63}{2} \times \frac{3}{14} = \frac{27}{4} = 6\frac{3}{4}\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 3480\text{ in.}^3\), \(B = 145\text{ in.}^2\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(3480 = 145h\). Divide both sides by \(145\) to find \(h = 24\text{ in.}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 70.2\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 4.5\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Using the formula \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(70.2 = 4.5h\). Divide both sides by \(4.5\) to find \(h = 15.6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 138.6\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 42\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Using \(V = Bh\), substitute the known values to get \(138.6 = 42h\). Dividing both sides by \(42\) yields \(h = 3.3\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 327.6\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 8.4\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Using \(V = Bh\), substitute the given values into \(327.6 = B(8.4)\). Dividing both sides by \(8.4\) gives \(B = 39\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 175.5\text{ mm}^3\), \(h = 6.5\text{ mm}\).
qs.s: Substitute into \(V = Bh\) to get \(175.5 = B(6.5)\). Dividing both sides by \(6.5\) gives \(B = 27\text{ mm}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 91.2\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 24\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Substitute into \(V = Bh\) to obtain \(91.2 = 24h\). Dividing both sides by \(24\) results in \(h = 3.8\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 388.8\text{ m}^3\), \(B = 72\text{ m}^2\).
qs.s: Substitute the given measurements into \(V = Bh\) to get \(388.8 = 72h\). Dividing both sides by \(72\) gives \(h = 5.4\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 18\frac{3}{8}\text{ cm}^3\), \(h = 2\frac{5}{8}\text{ cm}\).
qs.s: From \(V = Bh\), we have \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{147}{8} \div \frac{21}{8}\). Multiplying by the reciprocal yields \(\frac{147}{8} \times \frac{8}{21} = \frac{147}{21} = 7\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(V = 517.94\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 14.5\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Substitute the given measurements into \(V = Bh\) to get \(517.94 = B(14.5)\). Dividing \(517.94\) by \(14.5\) gives \(B = 35.72\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 22\frac{1}{2}\text{ m}^3\), \(B = 3\frac{1}{3}\text{ m}^2\).
qs.s: From \(V = Bh\), solve for \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{45}{2} \div \frac{10}{3}\). Multiplying by the reciprocal gives \(\frac{45}{2} \times \frac{3}{10} = \frac{27}{4} = 6\frac{3}{4}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 306.28\text{ cm}^3\), \(B = 24.8\text{ cm}^2\).
qs.s: Substitute the given measurements into \(V = Bh\) to get \(306.28 = 24.8h\). Dividing \(306.28\) by \(24.8\) gives \(h = 12.35\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V\) = Volume, \(B\) = area of base, and \(h\) = height of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(V = 15\frac{3}{4}\text{ m}^3\), \(B = 4\frac{1}{2}\text{ m}^2\).
qs.s: From \(V = Bh\), we have \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{63}{4} \div \frac{9}{2}\). Multiplying by the reciprocal gives \(\frac{63}{4} \times \frac{2}{9} = \frac{7}{2} = 3\frac{1}{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 70.56 cm³, B = 12.6 cm².
qs.s: Using the volume formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(h\) by dividing the volume by the base area: \(h = \frac{70.56}{12.6} = 5.6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: B, if V = 113.85 m³, h = 8.25 m.
qs.s: Using the volume formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(B\) by dividing the volume by the height: \(B = \frac{113.85}{8.25} = 13.8\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: V, if B = 14.8 m², h = 6.5 m.
qs.s: Using the volume formula \(V = Bh\), multiply the base area by the height: \(V = 14.8 \times 6.5 = 96.2\text{ m}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: B, if V = 68.4 ft³, h = 4.5 ft.
qs.s: Using the volume formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(B\) by dividing the volume by the height: \(B = \frac{68.4}{4.5} = 15.2\text{ ft}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 62.9 mm³, B = 18.5 mm².
qs.s: Using the volume formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(h\) by dividing the volume by the base area: \(h = \frac{62.9}{18.5} = 3.4\text{ mm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: V, if \(B = 3\frac{1}{3}\text{ in}^2\), \(h = 1\frac{5}{7}\text{ in}\).
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and multiply to find \(V\): \(V = Bh = \frac{10}{3} \times \frac{12}{7} = \frac{40}{7} = 5\frac{5}{7}\text{ in}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if \(V = 11\frac{2}{3}\text{ ft}^3\), \(B = 3\frac{1}{2}\text{ ft}^2\).
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and solve for \(h\): \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{35}{3} \div \frac{7}{2} = \frac{35}{3} \times \frac{2}{7} = \frac{10}{3} = 3\frac{1}{3}\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 1251.25 cm³, B = 38.5 cm².
qs.s: Divide the volume by the base area to determine the height: \(h = \frac{1251.25}{38.5} = 32.5\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: B, if \(V = 14\frac{2}{5}\text{ m}^3\), \(h = 2\frac{7}{10}\text{ m}\).
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and solve for \(B\): \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{72}{5} \div \frac{27}{10} = \frac{72}{5} \times \frac{10}{27} = \frac{16}{3} = 5\frac{1}{3}\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: B, if V = 1287.8 mm³, h = 23.5 mm.
qs.s: Divide the volume by the height to find the base area: \(B = \frac{1287.8}{23.5} = 54.8\text{ mm}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 86.4 cm³, B = 14.4 cm².
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, solve for height: h = V / B = 86.4 / 14.4 = 6 cm.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: B, if V = 117.5 cm³, h = 2.5 cm.
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, solve for base area: B = V / h = 117.5 / 2.5 = 47 cm².

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: V, if B = 21.6 cm², h = 3.5 cm.
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, multiply the base area by the height: V = 21.6 × 3.5 = 75.6 cm³.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: V, if B = 14.5 cm², h = 4.2 cm.
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, multiply the base area by the height: V = 14.5 × 4.2 = 60.9 cm³.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 102.6 cm³, B = 27 cm².
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, solve for height: h = V / B = 102.6 / 27 = 3.8 cm.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: B, if V = 52 1/2 cm³, h = 3 1/3 cm.
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and divide V by h: B = (105/2) ÷ (10/3) = (105/2) × (3/10) = 63/4 = 15 3/4 cm².

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: V, if B = 124.5 cm², h = 16.2 cm.
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, multiply the multi-digit decimals: V = 124.5 × 16.2 = 2016.9 cm³.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 1197 cm³, B = 68.4 cm².
qs.s: Using the formula V = Bh, divide the larger numbers to find the height: h = 1197 / 68.4 = 17.5 cm.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: V, if B = 6 2/3 cm², h = 4 1/4 cm.
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and multiply: V = (20/3) × (17/4) = 85/3 = 28 1/3 cm³.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if V = Volume, B = area of base, and h = height of a right rectangular prism: h, if V = 31 1/2 cm³, B = 4 2/3 cm².
qs.s: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions and divide V by B: h = (63/2) ÷ (14/3) = (63/2) × (3/14) = 27/4 = 6 3/4 cm.

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(h = 4.5\text{ m}\), \(V = 78.75\text{ m}^3\).
qs.s: Use the formula \(V = Bh\). Solving for \(B\) gives \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{78.75}{4.5} = 17.5\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(B = 8.5\text{ mm}^2\), \(V = 61.2\text{ mm}^3\).
qs.s: Use the formula \(V = Bh\). Solving for \(h\) gives \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{61.2}{8.5} = 7.2\text{ mm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(B = 14.5\text{ cm}^2\), \(V = 124.7\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: Use the formula \(V = Bh\). Solving for \(h\) gives \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{124.7}{14.5} = 8.6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(h = 7.2\text{ in}\), \(V = 97.92\text{ in}^3\).
qs.s: Use the formula \(V = Bh\). Solving for \(B\) gives \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{97.92}{7.2} = 13.6\text{ in}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(V\), if \(B = 12.4\text{ ft}^2\), \(h = 6.5\text{ ft}\).
qs.s: Use the formula \(V = Bh\). Substitute the given values to find \(V = 12.4 \times 6.5 = 80.6\text{ ft}^3\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if the rectangular base has length \(7.5\text{ cm}\) and width \(4.8\text{ cm}\), and \(V = 475.2\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: First calculate the base area: \(B = 7.5 \times 4.8 = 36\text{ cm}^2\). Then divide the volume by the base area: \(h = \frac{475.2}{36} = 13.2\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(h = 14.5\text{ cm}\), \(V = 2399.75\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: Using the volume formula \(V = Bh\), solve for \(B\) by dividing: \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{2399.75}{14.5} = 165.5\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(h\), if \(B = 4\frac{2}{3}\text{ m}^2\), \(V = 39\frac{2}{3}\text{ m}^3\).
qs.s: Convert to improper fractions: \(V = \frac{119}{3}\) and \(B = \frac{14}{3}\). Then divide to find the height: \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{119}{3} \div \frac{14}{3} = \frac{119}{14} = 8\frac{1}{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right prism: \(h\), if the base is composed of a rectangle of area \(36\text{ cm}^2\) and two triangles each of area \(18\text{ cm}^2\), and \(V = 864\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: Find the total base area by adding its parts: \(B = 36 + 18 + 18 = 72\text{ cm}^2\). Then find height using \(h = \frac{V}{B} = \frac{864}{72} = 12\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Find the unknown measurement, if \(V = \text{Volume}\), \(B = \text{area of base}\), and \(h = \text{height}\) of a right rectangular prism: \(B\), if \(h = 4x\) and \(V = 28x^3 + 16x^2 - 20x\).
qs.s: Divide the polynomial volume by the monomial height: \(B = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{28x^3 + 16x^2 - 20x}{4x} = 7x^2 + 4x - 5\).

exercises.name: Volume of a right prism from a diagram

qs.q: Use the diagram to find the volume of the right triangular prism.
qs.s: The base is a right triangle with area B = (1/2) × 8 cm × 6 cm = 24 cm². The volume of the prism is V = B × h = 24 cm² × 10 cm = 240 cm³.

qs.q: Use the diagram to find the volume of the right rectangular prism.
qs.s: The volume of a right rectangular prism is V = l × w × h. Multiplying the dimensions gives V = 8 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm = 160 cm³.

qs.q: Use the diagram to find the volume of the L-shaped right prism.

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a square base, a height of \(7\), and a volume of \(448\). What is its surface area?
qs.s: For a square base with side length \(s\), \(V = s^2 h\), so \(s^2 \times 7 = 448\), which gives \(s^2 = 64\) and \(s = 8\). The surface area is \(\text{SA} = 2s^2 + 4sh = 2(64) + 4(8)(7) = 128 + 224 = 352\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a height of \(5\) and a volume of \(360\). If its length is twice its width, what is its surface area?
qs.s: Let \(w\) be the width, so \(l = 2w\). Then \(V = (2w)(w)(5) = 10w^2 = 360\), giving \(w = 6\) and \(l = 12\). The surface area is \(\text{SA} = 2(12 \times 6 + 12 \times 5 + 6 \times 5) = 2(162) = 324\).

qs.q: A rectangular prism has a length of \(8\), a width of \(5\), and a total surface area of \(236\). What is its volume?

qs.q: A rectangular prism has length \(l = 8\), height \(h = 3\), and surface area \(SA = 180\). Find its volume \(V\).

qs.s: The area of one face is \(s^2 = 150 / 6 = 25\text{ cm}^2\), so the edge length is \(s = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ cm}\). The volume of the die is \(V = 5^3 = 125\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube, the surface area is listed as \(SA = 294\text{ cm}^2\). What is the volume \(V\) of the cube?
qs.s: Dividing the surface area by \(6\) gives the face area \(s^2 = 294 / 6 = 49\text{ cm}^2\), so the side length is \(s = \sqrt{49} = 7\text{ cm}\). The volume of the cube is \(V = s^3 = 7^3 = 343\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: A solid wooden block in the shape of a cube has a total surface area of \(96\text{ cm}^2\). What is the volume of the block?
qs.s: The area of one face is \(s^2 = 96 / 6 = 16\text{ cm}^2\), which gives a side length of \(s = \sqrt{16} = 4\text{ cm}\). Therefore, the volume is \(V = 4^3 = 64\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: A cubic storage crate has a total surface area of \(486\text{ ft}^2\). What is the volume of the crate?
qs.s: Each face has an area of \(s^2 = 486 / 6 = 81\text{ ft}^2\), giving an edge length of \(s = \sqrt{81} = 9\text{ ft}\). Thus, the volume is \(V = 9^3 = 729\text{ ft}^3\).

qs.q: A cubic gift box has a total surface area of \(384\text{ in.}^2\). What is the volume of the box?
qs.s: Dividing the total surface area by \(6\) gives \(s^2 = 384 / 6 = 64\text{ in.}^2\), so the side length is \(s = \sqrt{64} = 8\text{ in.}\) The volume is \(V = 8^3 = 512\text{ in.}^3\).

qs.q: Two cubes have total surface areas of \(150\text{ cm}^2\) and \(600\text{ cm}^2\), respectively. What is the difference between their volumes?
qs.s: The side lengths are \(s_1 = \sqrt{150 / 6} = 5\text{ cm}\) and \(s_2 = \sqrt{600 / 6} = 10\text{ cm}\), giving volumes of \(V_1 = 5^3 = 125\text{ cm}^3\) and \(V_2 = 10^3 = 1000\text{ cm}^3\). The difference in volume is \(1000 - 125 = 875\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: A large cubic shipping container has a total surface area of \(1350\text{ cm}^2\). What is the volume of the container?
qs.s: Dividing the total surface area by \(6\) gives \(s^2 = 1350 / 6 = 225\text{ cm}^2\), so the edge length is \(s = \sqrt{225} = 15\text{ cm}\). The volume is \(V = 15^3 = 3375\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: A cube has a total surface area of \(216\text{ cm}^2\). If each edge of the cube is increased by \(2\text{ cm}\), what is the volume of the new cube?
qs.s: The original side length is \(s = \sqrt{216 / 6} = 6\text{ cm}\), so the new edge length is \(6 + 2 = 8\text{ cm}\). The volume of the new cube is \(V = 8^3 = 512\text{ cm}^3\).

qs.q: A cube has a total surface area of \(\frac{8}{3}\text{ m}^2\). What is the volume of the cube?
qs.s: The area of one face is \(s^2 = \frac{8}{3} \div 6 = \frac{4}{9}\text{ m}^2\), so the side length is \(s = \sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ m}\). Thus, the volume is \(V = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3 = \frac{8}{27}\text{ m}^3\).

qs.q: For \(x > 0\), a cube has a total surface area of \(24x^2\). What is the volume of the cube in terms of \(x\)?
qs.s: The area of one face is \(s^2 = \frac{24x^2}{6} = 4x^2\), so the edge length is \(s = \sqrt{4x^2} = 2x\). The volume of the cube is \(V = (2x)^3 = 8x^3\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube with side length \(S\), surface area \(SA\), and volume \(V\), the volume is given as \(V = 64\). What is the value of \(SA\)?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4\). Then the surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(4^2) = 6(16) = 96\).

qs.q: For a cube of side length \(S\), surface area \(SA\), and volume \(V\), if \(V = 1000\), find the surface area \(SA\).
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{1000} = 10\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(10^2) = 600\).

qs.q: A cube-shaped storage box has a volume of \(27\text{ cm}^3\). What is its total surface area in square centimeters?
qs.s: The side length of the box is \(S = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\text{ cm}\). The total surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(3^2) = 54\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube with side length \(S\), surface area \(SA\), and volume \(V\), a row has \(V = 8\). What is the corresponding value of \(SA\)?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(2^2) = 24\).

qs.q: A solid cube has a volume of \(343\text{ mm}^3\). What is its total surface area in square millimeters?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{343} = 7\text{ mm}\). The total surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(7^2) = 294\text{ mm}^2\).

qs.q: A cubic container has a volume of \(V = 8000\text{ cm}^3\). What is its total surface area in square centimeters?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{8000} = 20\text{ cm}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(20^2) = 2400\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube with side length \(S\), surface area \(SA\), and volume \(V\), a row gives the volume as \(V = \frac{27}{64}\). What is the surface area \(SA\) in simplest form?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{64}} = \frac{3}{4}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 = 6\left(\frac{9}{16}\right) = \frac{27}{8}\).

qs.q: A cube has a volume of \(V = 0.064\text{ m}^3\). What is its total surface area in square meters?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{0.064} = 0.4\text{ m}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6(0.4^2) = 6(0.16) = 0.96\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube with side length \(S\), surface area \(SA\), and volume \(V\), the surface area is given as \(SA = \frac{3}{2}\). What is the volume \(V\) of the cube in simplest form?
qs.s: Since \(SA = 6S^2 = \frac{3}{2}\), dividing by 6 gives \(S^2 = \frac{1}{4}\), so \(S = \frac{1}{2}\). The volume is \(V = S^3 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube of side length \(S\), surface area \(SA\), and volume \(V\), a row has \(V = 512\). What is the value of \(S + SA\)?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{512} = 8\), and the surface area is \(SA = 6(8^2) = 384\). Thus, \(S + SA = 8 + 384 = 392\).

qs.q: A cubic gift box has a volume of \(729\text{ cm}^3\). Find the total surface area of the box.
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{729} = 9\text{ cm}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times 9^2 = 486\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube of side length \(S\), the volume is recorded as \(V = 125\text{ cm}^3\). What is the surface area, \(SA\), of the cube?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{125} = 5\text{ cm}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times 5^2 = 150\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A solid wooden cube has a volume of \(512\text{ cm}^3\). What is the total surface area of the cube?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{512} = 8\text{ cm}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times 8^2 = 384\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A cube-shaped block of cheese has a volume of \(27\text{ cm}^3\). What is the total surface area of the block?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\text{ cm}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times 3^2 = 54\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A cubic storage container has a volume of \(64\text{ m}^3\). What is its total surface area?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4\text{ m}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times 4^2 = 96\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: A large cubic water tank has a volume of \(1331\text{ m}^3\). What is the total surface area of the tank?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{1331} = 11\text{ m}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times 11^2 = 726\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: A cube has a volume of \(216\text{ cm}^3\). If each edge of the cube is increased by \(4\text{ cm}\), what is the total surface area of the enlarged cube?
qs.s: The original edge length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{216} = 6\text{ cm}\), so the enlarged edge length is \(6 + 4 = 10\text{ cm}\). The new surface area is \(SA = 6 \times 10^2 = 600\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A small cubic crystal has a volume of \(\frac{125}{27}\text{ cm}^3\). What is its total surface area?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{\frac{125}{27}} = \frac{5}{3}\text{ cm}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6 \times \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^2 = 6 \times \frac{25}{9} = \frac{50}{3}\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A cubic block of foam has a volume of \(0.064\text{ m}^3\). What is the total surface area of the block?
qs.s: The side length is \(S = \sqrt[3]{0.064} = 0.4\text{ m}\). The surface area is \(SA = 6S^2 = 6 \times (0.4)^2 = 0.96\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: Cube A has a volume of \(512\text{ cm}^3\) and Cube B has a volume of \(64\text{ cm}^3\). How much greater is the total surface area of Cube A than the total surface area of Cube B?
qs.s: Cube A has side length \(8\text{ cm}\) and surface area \(6 \times 8^2 = 384\text{ cm}^2\). Cube B has side length \(4\text{ cm}\) and surface area \(6 \times 4^2 = 96\text{ cm}^2\). The difference is \(384 - 96 = 288\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube (with columns \(S\), \(\text{SA}\), and \(V\)), find the surface area \(\text{SA}\) given that the side length is \(S = 10m\).
qs.s: The surface area of a cube is \(\text{SA} = 6S^2 = 6(10m)^2 = 6(100m^2) = 600m^2\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube (with columns \(S\), \(\text{SA}\), and \(V\)), find the volume \(V\) given that the side length is \(S = 4p\).
qs.s: The volume of a cube is \(V = S^3 = (4p)^3 = 64p^3\).

qs.q: In a table of measurements for a cube (with columns \(S\), \(\text{SA}\), and \(V\)), find the surface area \(\text{SA}\) given that the side length is \(S = 5a\).
